paragraphs: This paper studies transformer mistakes through semantic dependencies: relationships in which one word’s meaning depends on another. The researchers examine how token representations change when sentence meaning changes, using question answering to connect internal representations with model behavior. Their experiments cover models from the BERT family, GPT, and LLaMA.

The analysis finds that most tokens largely preserve their original semantic information as they pass through successive layers. At the same time, tokens in the final layer can encode correct relationships between meanings. These findings suggest that retaining information about an individual word and representing its relationship to other words can coexist inside a transformer.

Incorrect answers often involve particular tokens that encode the wrong semantic dependencies. Fixing these errors by directly changing parameters is difficult because the same parameters can represent correct relationships in one context and incorrect ones in another. The contribution is an interpretable account of some answer failures, together with evidence that their causes depend on context.
icml-2025-a-lens-into-interpretable-tran.tldr: Transformer answer errors often involve tokens encoding incorrect semantic relationships, whose context dependence makes direct parameter fixes difficult.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning methods can learn slowly when their estimates of action values are biased. These Q-values represent how rewarding actions are expected to be, so overestimating them can distort learning. The paper focuses on reducing this overestimation, a mechanism the authors identify as contributing to the success of several modern reinforcement learning algorithms.

ADDQ builds on distributional reinforcement learning, which represents a distribution of possible returns. Its central idea is to handle overestimation in a locally adaptive way. This makes the adjustment responsive to local circumstances within learning. The authors present the framework as straightforward to integrate into existing distributional implementations, requiring only a small amount of additional code.

The work combines theoretical support with experiments in tabular environments, Atari, and MuJoCo, including comparisons with leading methods. It also proves convergence in the tabular case. That guarantee has a specific scope: it supports convergence for the tabular setting, while the broader experiments examine how the framework behaves in more complex environments.
icml-2025-addq-adaptive-distributional-d.tldr: ADDQ adds a locally adaptive overestimation correction to distributional reinforcement learning, with a convergence proof for the tabular setting.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model reduces its memory and computational requirements, but ordinary language benchmarks may miss changes in its ability to act as an agent. This paper introduces ACBench to evaluate capabilities such as generating workflows, using tools, understanding long contexts, and handling real-world applications. The aim is to assess whether efficiency gains preserve the behaviors needed in these settings.

The benchmark includes 12 tasks spanning four capability areas and evaluates 15 models, covering small models, standard models, and distilled reasoning models. It examines two forms of compression: 4-bit quantization using GPTQ or AWQ, and 50% pruning using Wanda or SparseGPT. This design allows the evaluation to compare compression effects across tasks and model types.

The experiments find that 4-bit quantization produces reported drops of 1%–3% for workflow generation and tool use, while real-world application accuracy drops by 10%–15%. The authors also introduce ERank, Top-k Ranking Correlation, and Energy for analysis. The results show why preserving one agent capability does not establish that compression preserves the others.
icml-2025-can-compressed-llms-truly-act-.tldr: ACBench finds that compression affects agent capabilities unevenly, with 4-bit quantization preserving some skills better than real-world application accuracy.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization occurs when a larger student learns from labels generated by a weaker teacher and can outperform that teacher. This paper investigates the phenomenon through the observation that fine-tuning often takes place in a space with relatively few effective dimensions. It analyzes a ridgeless regression setting to understand how training on teacher labels can reduce variance.

For sufficiently expressive, low-dimensional student and teacher feature spaces, the authors exactly characterize the variance that dominates generalization error. Teacher variance is inherited in the feature space shared by both models. In the part of the teacher’s feature space outside the student’s, it is reduced by a factor equal to the student space’s dimension divided by the number of pseudo-labels.

This distinction explains how differences between teacher and student representations can help under the analyzed conditions. It also connects the amount of training data to variance reduction and recovery of the performance gap. Experiments on synthetic regression, vision, and language tasks support the analysis, linking the theoretical account to observed weak-to-strong behavior.
icml-2025-discrepancies-are-virtue-weak-.tldr: A low-dimensional regression analysis shows how differences between teacher and student feature spaces can reduce inherited variance in weak-to-strong learning.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves an optimization problem whose outcome depends on another optimization problem. It appears in applications such as choosing hyperparameters and meta-learning. Gradient-based approaches need hypergradients, which describe how the outer objective changes through the inner problem. Computing useful approximations to these quantities is therefore central to making such approaches efficient.

This paper proposes an efficient way to incorporate curvature information into hypergradient approximation. Curvature describes how gradients change, providing information beyond a local direction of improvement. The authors build an algorithmic framework around the enhanced approximation, carefully exploiting hypergradient structure together with an inexact Newton method to reduce the computational effort required.

The framework comes with convergence-rate guarantees in both deterministic and stochastic settings. The stated improvement in computational complexity over popular gradient-based methods applies specifically to the deterministic setting. Numerical experiments also demonstrate substantial practical benefits from including curvature. Together, these results support using additional local information when it can be incorporated economically into the hypergradient computation.
icml-2025-efficient-curvature-aware-hype.tldr: An efficient curvature-aware hypergradient approximation improves deterministic bilevel optimization complexity and delivers practical benefits in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Language models are trained to predict the next token, yet this paper argues that their internal representations contain information about much later parts of a response. The researchers use simple probes to investigate what can be recovered from the model’s representation of a prompt. Their focus is on properties of the response as a whole.

The probes reveal information about several kinds of future attributes. Structural attributes include response length and the number of reasoning steps. Content attributes include characters chosen for a story and a multiple-choice answer appearing at the end. Behavioral attributes include answer confidence and factual consistency. These findings indicate that prompt representations can carry information extending beyond the immediate next token.

The study also examines how this response planning varies with model size across tasks and how it changes during generation. The authors interpret the evidence as emergent planning in hidden representations. They suggest that these signals could support greater transparency and control over generation, presenting those applications as potential uses of the findings.
icml-2025-emergent-response-planning-in-.tldr: Probes reveal that LLM prompt representations encode attributes of future responses, providing evidence of emergent response planning.

paragraphs: Avoiding Undesired Future asks how to choose actions when a machine learning model predicts an unwanted outcome. Rehearsal learning provides a framework for reasoning about uncertainty in this decision problem. This paper addresses a remaining question: under what conditions can an action that maximizes the probability of avoiding the outcome be identified?

The authors introduce CARE, short for CAnonical REctangle, as a condition under which the maximum avoidance probability can be achieved. They develop a projection-Newton algorithm for selecting actions and prove that, under CARE, it converges superlinearly to an optimal action. This links an explicit condition on the problem to both optimality and a strong convergence result.

The paper also provides a way to adapt the algorithm to scenarios beyond CARE. Separately, it establishes a closed-form solution when the outcome consists of a single variable, substantially reducing decision-making time complexity. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness and efficiency. The strongest stated convergence guarantee remains tied to CARE, while the extension broadens where the approach can be used.
icml-2025-enabling-optimal-decisions-in-.tldr: Under the CARE condition, a projection-Newton algorithm converges superlinearly to an action maximizing the probability of avoiding an unwanted outcome.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can rely on spurious correlations, associating a prediction with image features that are incidental to the intended concept. Existing approaches often use labeled fine-tuning or increasingly elaborate prompts generated by language models. ERICT addresses the problem during inference by using concept information to guide the model’s visual attention.

The method first uses auxiliary prompts to identify concept tokens that capture invariant features and builds a token-level mask. It then applies this mask to attention weights associated with the vision encoder’s CLS token. This directs the model toward image regions relevant to the concept, putting the visual representation at the center of the robustness intervention.

The experiments report significant gains in overall performance and in performance for the worst-performing group, alongside new state-of-the-art results. The group-level finding matters because an aggregate improvement alone can leave poorly served groups behind. ERICT’s contribution is an inference-stage mechanism that connects identifying relevant concepts with changing where the vision encoder attends.
icml-2025-erict-enhancing-robustness-by-.tldr: ERICT uses concept-based attention masks during inference to reduce spurious correlations and improve overall and worst-group vision-language performance.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds connect a learning algorithm’s performance on its training sample with its expected performance on the underlying population. Information-theoretic approaches have been useful for randomized algorithms, but existing bounds can be overly large or converge slowly. This paper develops new bounds using a binary variant of Jensen-Shannon divergence.

A foundational lemma describes the relationship between an arbitrary variable and a binary variable. From it, the authors derive hypothesis-based bounds that improve conditional mutual information bounds while reducing the number of conditioned samples from two to one. They also establish prediction-based bounds that improve on earlier approaches using mutual information of evaluated losses.

A further technique converts evaluated loss variables into a binary form and yields exactly tight generalization bounds for general randomized learning algorithms with bounded losses. The results address limitations of previous analyses for certain stochastic convex optimization problems. They do so without additional assumptions that the algorithm is stable or compressible, making bounded loss a key part of the stated scope.
icml-2025-exactly-tight-information-theo.tldr: Binary Jensen-Shannon divergence yields exactly tight generalization bounds for randomized learning with bounded losses, without added stability or compressibility assumptions.

paragraphs: Standard diffusion models add isotropic Gaussian noise during their forward process, an approach naturally suited to Euclidean geometry. This paper considers data arranged on a hypersphere, where angular relationships describe important class-specific structure. Treating these distributions as Euclidean can lose distinctions encoded by direction and lead to poorer generation.

HyperSphereDiff introduces directional noise to align the diffusion process with hyperspherical structure. Its goal is to preserve class geometry while representing uncertainty in angle. This matters because the relevant variation is organized around directions and angular regions, so the noise process should reflect the geometry the model is meant to learn.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that the approach better aligns generation with the data’s intrinsic geometry. They evaluate it on four object datasets and two face datasets, reporting improved preservation of the underlying hyperspherical manifold through angular uncertainty modeling. The contribution is a geometry-aware diffusion framework supported by evidence for the hyperspherical setting studied.
icml-2025-harmonizing-geometry-and-uncer.tldr: HyperSphereDiff uses directional noise to model angular uncertainty and better preserve the geometry of hyperspherical data.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can classify unseen categories through text descriptions, but adversarial inputs can disrupt their predictions. Adversarial fine-tuning commonly aligns an attacked example’s prediction scores with those of its clean counterpart. This paper argues that intermediate examples along the attack trajectory contain valuable information about the decision boundary that this approach typically overlooks.

The authors consider simplices formed from a clean example and two consecutive points on the adversarial trajectory. Sampling within these regions would expose training to a broader local decision landscape, but doing so is expensive. They use a Taylor expansion to formulate an upper bound on alignment loss involving the Jacobian and Hessian at clean examples.

The resulting closed-form formulation is equivalent to infinite uniform sampling of the simplex within that formulation, avoiding explicit sampling of all those candidates. The method reports state-of-the-art robustness across 15 datasets and diverse vision-language tasks. Its central contribution is an efficient way to incorporate information from regions connecting clean inputs and intermediate adversarial examples.
icml-2025-improving-zero-shot-adversaria.tldr: A closed-form alignment formulation uses regions along adversarial trajectories to improve zero-shot vision-language robustness without costly explicit simplex sampling.

paragraphs: The paper studies a transformer trained on recorded interactions from multiple reinforcement learning tasks and then used, with fixed parameters, to produce actions for new tasks. The challenge is that historical data may come from policies that make poor decisions. Ordinary autoregressive training then imitates those policies, carrying their shortcomings into the learned behavior.

The Decision Importance Transformer addresses this by reproducing an actor-critic approach through in-context learning. First, a transformer-based value function estimates advantages for the policies that generated the data. These estimates characterize which decisions were relatively beneficial. A second transformer learns the policy through weighted maximum likelihood, with the value estimates determining how strongly different training decisions influence learning.

The weighting is designed to steer learning from suboptimal behavior toward optimal policies. Experiments on bandit problems and Markov decision processes report superior performance, especially when historical trajectories are suboptimal. The findings support using estimated decision quality to learn more effectively from imperfect experience, while preserving the setup in which the trained transformer stays fixed on new tasks.
icml-2025-in-context-reinforcement-learn.tldr: Decision Importance Transformer uses advantage-weighted training to improve in-context reinforcement learning from suboptimal historical trajectories.

paragraphs: Length generalization is the ability to handle sequences longer than those encountered during training. This paper approaches the problem through a language model’s output distributions. It asks whether consistency between outputs on shorter and longer sequences can help explain why some models extend to greater lengths more effectively.

Synthetic task studies highlight long-short alignment: consistency of output distributions across sequence lengths. The authors then introduce Long-Short Misalignment, a metric for measuring this behavior in natural language tasks. They find a strong correlation between the metric and length generalization performance, making output behavior a useful signal for studying the problem.

Building on this observation, the paper develops a training regularizer that encourages alignment across lengths. Extensive experiments support the approach’s effectiveness for long-context modeling. The work thus connects a diagnostic observation with a training intervention: measure how output distributions diverge across lengths, then encourage greater consistency. The reported correlation motivates this strategy, while the experiments provide evidence for the intervention itself.
icml-2025-long-short-alignment-for-effec.tldr: Aligning output distributions across short and long sequences provides a useful diagnostic and an effective training regularizer for length generalization.

paragraphs: Multiwinner voting selects a fixed-size committee from people’s preferences over candidates. This paper studies what happens when the candidate set changes as candidates arrive or leave. A committee must continue to satisfy a proportionality requirement, while avoiding excessive changes from the previous selection. Representation and continuity therefore become simultaneous algorithmic goals.

The authors examine three settings: approval preferences, ranked preferences, and proportional clustering. For different proportionality axioms, they either construct algorithms that make few changes or establish that such algorithms cannot exist. This makes the specific representation requirement central to determining whether a stable update procedure is possible.

For ranked preferences, the paper establishes impossibility of the desired low-change algorithms in the studied setting. For approval preferences and proportional clustering, it provides amortized and exact algorithms for several proportionality notions. Amortized guarantees concern behavior over a sequence of updates. The results map where proportional representation can be maintained with limited disruption as the available candidates change.
icml-2025-maintaining-proportional-commi.tldr: The paper identifies when proportional committees can be updated with few changes as candidates join or leave, and when this is impossible.

paragraphs: Many self-supervised learning methods compare representations using cosine similarity, which depends on vector direction. This appears to make vector length, or embedding norm, irrelevant. Yet earlier observations connected norms with learning behavior and confidence. This paper investigates that apparent contradiction and develops a systematic account of the norm’s role during training.

Using theory, simulations, and experiments, the authors show that embedding norms govern convergence rates. They also find that norms encode network confidence, with smaller norms corresponding to unexpected samples. Thus, a quantity absent from the direct similarity comparison can still carry information about both how the network learns and how it responds to an input.

The study further shows that manipulating embedding norms can substantially change convergence speed. That finding gives norms practical relevance as well as interpretive value. The contribution is to connect representation geometry, training dynamics, and confidence, explaining why understanding self-supervised models requires attention to the lengths of their embeddings even when their similarity measure emphasizes direction.
icml-2025-on-the-importance-of-embedding.tldr: Embedding norms affect self-supervised learning speed and encode confidence even when models compare embeddings using cosine similarity.

paragraphs: Generating several responses and combining them through majority voting or best-of-N selection can improve language model accuracy. The temperature used for sampling strongly affects the results, making its selection an important part of this process. Common approaches use a fixed value or tune it on labeled validation examples, which may be difficult to obtain.

This paper studies how to identify a near-optimal temperature for multi-sample aggregation without task-specific validation data. Its analysis examines variation across model architectures, model sizes, datasets, task types, and predictive accuracy. This broadens the question from choosing a single default to understanding how useful temperature choices depend on the model and task.

The authors propose an entropy-based metric for automatic temperature optimization and report that it consistently outperforms fixed-temperature baselines. They also introduce a stochastic process model to help interpret the relationship between temperature and performance. Together, the selection metric and explanatory model offer a more systematic way to configure multi-sample inference when labeled tuning data are scarce.
icml-2025-optimizing-temperature-for-lan.tldr: An entropy-based method automatically selects temperature for multi-sample language model inference without task-specific validation data, outperforming fixed-temperature baselines.

paragraphs: Tests of cross-covariance matrix rank help causal discovery by revealing relationships that can include information about latent variables. Existing tests often assume continuous quantities are measured directly. In practice, a continuous trait may only be recorded through ordered categories, such as disagreement, neutrality, or agreement. This discretization can undermine the tests’ statistical error control.

The paper introduces Mixed data Permutation-based Rank Test, or MPRT, for settings where some or all variables have been discretized. Its theoretical analysis establishes exchangeability and uses permutations to estimate the asymptotic distribution expected under the null hypothesis. This provides the basis for controlling Type I error, meaning false rejection of that hypothesis.

The authors show that MPRT can maintain this error control in the presence of discretization where previous methods cannot. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support both its effectiveness and its use in causal discovery. The contribution is a rank-testing approach that explicitly accounts for how variables are observed, helping preserve valid inference with mixed measurements.
icml-2025-permutation-based-rank-test-in.tldr: MPRT uses permutations to control rank-test false positives when continuous variables are observed through discretized categories.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often assumes feedback after every state-action pair, but collecting such detailed rewards can be costly. This paper studies an intermediate arrangement between step-by-step feedback and a single evaluation of an entire trajectory. Each episode is divided into a chosen number of segments, with feedback supplied only when a segment ends.

The researchers analyze two feedback types within an episodic Markov decision process. Binary feedback provides a binary outcome for a segment, while sum feedback supplies its accumulated reward. They develop efficient algorithms and establish upper and lower regret bounds to determine how the number of segments changes learning performance.

The results show a sharp difference between these feedback types. With binary feedback, increasing the segment count decreases regret at an exponential rate in the studied model. With summed rewards, increasing the count brings no significant regret reduction. Theory and experiments support this distinction, showing that the usefulness of more frequent feedback depends strongly on what information each feedback signal contains.
icml-2025-reinforcement-learning-with-se.tldr: More frequent segment feedback greatly reduces regret with binary outcomes, but offers little regret improvement when feedback already gives reward sums.

paragraphs: Sleeping Reinforcement Learning studies environments where available actions change during interaction. Availability may depend on the environment, constraints, or external randomness. The paper asks how difficult learning becomes when an agent cannot assume that every action remains available, and shows that the timing and structure of availability information are crucial.

When available action sets are revealed at the start of each episode, a modified UCBVI algorithm achieves regret of order H times the square root of SAT, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here H is the episode horizon, S and A count states and actions, and T is the learning horizon. Revealing availability only at each decision can be much harder.

For availability governed by a Markovian process, the authors establish a minimax lower bound of order the square root of T times 2 raised to A/2. This exposes a statistical barrier involving the action count. When availability depends only on the current state and stage, an optimistic algorithm recovers the earlier regret order, matching standard reinforcement learning complexity in that restricted setting.
icml-2025-sleeping-reinforcement-learnin.tldr: Learning with changing action availability can match standard RL complexity under restricted conditions, while more general availability creates a severe statistical barrier.

paragraphs: Training language models to prove formal theorems is constrained by the supply of correct proofs. Repeatedly generating proofs and training on successful ones can plateau when successes become scarce. The Self-play Theorem Prover addresses this by giving the model two interacting roles: proposing conjectures and attempting to prove them.

The conjecturer learns from previously generated statements that the current prover can barely solve. This encourages increasingly challenging exercises as the prover improves. The prover trains through expert iteration on successful proofs of these conjectures. The two roles therefore supply training opportunities for each other, creating an evolving source of problems near the prover’s current ability.

The authors evaluate STP with Lean and Isabelle. After generating 51.3 billion training tokens in Lean, STP proves 28.5% of LeanWorkbook statements, compared with the previous expert-iteration result of 13.1%. At pass@3200, the final model reports leading whole-proof generation results of 65.0% on miniF2F-test, 23.9% on ProofNet-test, and 8 of 644 on PutnamBench. These results support self-generated conjectures as a way to extend training progress.
icml-2025-stp-self-play-llm-theorem-prov.tldr: STP improves formal theorem proving through self-play between a conjecturer that proposes challenging statements and a prover that learns to solve them.

paragraphs: In network data, an individual’s outcome can depend on their own treatment and on interactions with peers. This makes causal estimation difficult, especially when different peer effects are combined. The paper introduces a setting that distinguishes direct peer effects, indirect peer effects, and the effect of the individual’s own treatment.

The authors provide identification conditions for these effects and adapt causal mediation analysis to network data. Their estimation approach uses attention to represent differences in how strongly neighbors influence an individual. Multiple graph neural network layers capture higher-order neighbor effects. The method also incorporates the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion to improve robustness and accuracy.

Experiments use two semi-synthetic datasets derived from real networks and a recommendation-system dataset, supporting the approach’s effectiveness. Separating different pathways of influence could help decision-makers design interventions in connected populations. The identification conditions are central to the causal interpretation: the framework specifies when the distinct effects can be identified, while the model addresses the practical challenge of estimating them in networks.
icml-2025-telling-peer-direct-effects-fr.tldr: A network-specific causal mediation framework separates direct and indirect peer effects from own-treatment effects, with identification conditions and empirical support.

paragraphs: Textual unlearning aims to make language models forget selected training texts, including sensitive information. This paper examines whether existing methods actually provide the expected privacy protection. Its focus is on whether a text remains detectable after unlearning and whether deploying unlearning mechanisms can expose additional information about the targeted material.

The authors introduce U-LiRA+, an auditing method that finds unlearned texts can still be detected with very high confidence. They then develop the Textual Unlearning Leakage Attack, or TULA, with variants for both black-box and white-box access. These attacks investigate privacy risks under different levels of access to the model.

The findings show that textual unlearning mechanisms could reveal more about the texts they are supposed to remove, creating membership inference and reconstruction risks. Membership inference concerns whether a particular text was present, while reconstruction concerns recovering its content. The paper therefore challenges the reliability of the evaluated unlearning mechanisms and motivates approaches whose privacy claims withstand direct auditing.
icml-2025-textual-unlearning-gives-a-fal.tldr: Audits and leakage attacks show that existing textual unlearning can leave texts detectable and may expose additional information about them.

paragraphs: Sparse dictionary learning has been used to extract meaningful concepts from language model internals. This paper asks whether it can also reveal useful concepts in microscopy foundation models. The challenge differs from interpreting ordinary text because scientific images are less directly understandable, and researchers may have limited prior knowledge of the high-level concepts a model represents.

The proposed method combines Iterative Codebook Feature Learning, a sparse dictionary learning algorithm, with PCA whitening based on control data. This preprocessing and feature-learning combination is applied to representations from models trained on cell microscopy images. The aim is to extract interpretable biological structure from the model’s internal features.

The researchers recover concepts associated with cell types and genetic perturbations. They also show how the method reveals subtle changes in cell morphology arising from interpretable interventions. These results support dictionary learning as a promising tool for mechanistic interpretation in bioimaging, with potential to aid scientific discovery by exposing biologically meaningful distinctions already encoded in learned representations.
icml-2025-towards-scientific-discovery-w.tldr: Sparse dictionary learning with control-derived PCA whitening extracts biological concepts and subtle morphological changes from microscopy model representations.

paragraphs: Human preferences can be easier to provide than a numerical reward function, but translating them into sequential decisions raises theoretical questions. This paper connects preferences over trajectories, utilities that may depend on an entire history, and Markovian rewards. It models preferences as a partial preorder, allowing some trajectories to be incomparable.

The authors define compatibility between preferences and multi-objective utilities, then study the difficulty of constructing such representations. Finding a utility with the minimum number of dimensions is NP-hard. They also introduce preference-based policy dominance, allowing policies to be compared without first assigning utilities or rewards, and examine the computational complexity of assessing that relationship.

Finally, the paper develops an efficient algorithm for approximating a utility with Markovian rewards. It measures approximation error through the suboptimality of the policy chosen using the resulting reward. This ties representation quality to decision quality. The framework offers a principled foundation for learning from preferences while retaining incomparability and making the costs of translating preferences explicit.
icml-2025-towards-theoretical-understand.tldr: The paper formalizes links between partial preferences, utilities, and rewards, including computational barriers and an efficient reward-approximation method.

paragraphs: Inferring types in Python is challenging because programs can operate without explicit type annotations. This paper introduces TypyBench to evaluate how well language models infer types across entire repositories. The broader scope matters because an individually plausible type prediction must also fit with how values and functions are used throughout the codebase.

TypyBench introduces two complementary metrics. TypeSim measures semantic relationships between a predicted type and the reference type, recognizing more than exact textual agreement. TypeCheck assesses consistency across the repository. Together, these metrics separate the question of whether a prediction resembles the expected type from whether the collection of predictions works coherently across the program.

Evaluations on 50 curated Python repositories find that models achieve decent TypeSim scores but struggle with complex nested types and produce substantial consistency errors. The results suggest that better local similarity alone will not resolve repository-level inference problems. The benchmark supports a research focus on types that remain compatible across their different usage contexts.
icml-2025-typybench-evaluating-llm-type-.tldr: TypyBench finds that plausible Python type predictions can still be inconsistent across repositories, highlighting a gap in LLM type inference.
